svg.title: 3. Identity, secrets and detection
svg.text: How the shop is meant to authenticate
Workloads: pods in AKS, no secrets anywhere
The attack (one legacy app still had a client secret)
Why the attacker got nothing, and what changed afterwards
Scenario: a client secret leaks to a public repo. What stops the attacker, what detects them, and what cleans up
Risk-based policy: high user risk → "Require risk remediation".
The user changes password, sessions are revoked, attacker's
refresh tokens die. Break-glass accounts are excluded and alarmed.
Token exchange: Kubernetes SA token → Entra token. Nothing to leak.
sp-reporting secret pushed to a public GitHub repo by
a contractor. The app reads order totals for finance.
Attacker gets a token for sp-reporting from a TOR exit
node. The secret is valid, so Entra ID issues it.
Calls kv-data-weu to list secrets: 403. Public network
access is disabled; only the private endpoint answers.
Calls Azure Resource Manager with the role it has
the SQL server, tries the public endpoint: refused.
Entra ID Protection matches the secret it found on
1. Disable sp-reporting, remove all its credentials
2. Rotate every secret it could read, from Key Vault logs
3. Add the IP to the Front Door WAF block list
4. Page on-call, open a ticket with the evidence
Private endpoints with public network access
Disabled on Key Vault, SQL, Cosmos DB and
Storage. A valid token is not enough: the
request also has to come from inside the VNet.
Defender for Key Vault flagged denied access
from a suspicious IP. ID Protection flagged
the leaked secret. Sentinel joined both with
the sign-in logs into one incident.
sp-reporting had a 2-year secret and no
A location policy would have refused the
token request from outside known IPs.
Reporting job moved into AKS with workload
identity (no secret). An Entra app management
policy blocks new client secrets, and GitHub
push protection stops secrets at commit time.
Same pattern for a phished engineer: risk-based Conditional Access revokes sessions, PIM means no standing Owner role to steal, and every activation is logged.
Alert names are from the Defender for Cloud alert reference. The timeline is illustrative; ID Protection's leaked-credentials check runs offline, so it can lag the attacker by hours.
